title: No Country For Old Men is the “Watchmen” of Action Films and people don’t even realize it.

I think you are onto some edges of themes here, but this isn’t about the movies. Llewelyn is a tough guy in a tough world, but also an ordinary guy going nowhere. He sees his one chance to land a bunch of money and takes it. It’s Americana and the Old West, making his play for a stake in the world. And you know what? He makes it pretty far. But ultimately this world is much bigger and tougher and swallows him up.
You know watchmen was a critically acclaimed graph novel first and foremost right?

Watchmen the comic- rightfully lauded as one of the most important literary works of the past few decades?- or Watchmen the movie -one of the 21st century's bold but highly contentious films, of which was released after the coen Brothers film came out? 

Having navigated through the film school essay metaphoric machine, I think this has all the energy of a third year deadline cram, where because something feels analogous and rhetorically dense, it's all squashed onto the page in this kind of desperate rallying cry of "I'm not sure if this is true or not, but it sounds good on the printed page."

I guess this is the magic of cinema. Sometimes a lack of words gives you a canvas to fill it with your own imagination and interpretation based on your experiences.

Llewelyn was a war veteran. He was smart, resourceful and methodical and very cautious. He was never cocky or arrogant about his skills, he just solved his problems, oftentimes quite successfully. He never mentioned that he feels safe or comfortable in the situation, he rarely let his guard down. 

If your assumptions were correct about his false sense of reality, he would have vocalised it many times how heroic he is or how everything is gonna be alright, just like in the movies. That would be a totally different movie, but i guess that could have tell a similar story. But it was not the intention of the writers. It was a very capable man doing his best despite the odds and failing, because life is not just. It can be harsh and cruel and random and can beat the best of us without warning.

He's not going back because he sees himself as a hero, he just feels remorse and guilt for his selfishness. And his only selfless act in the whole movie will lead him to his doom. Kinda similarly to Barry Lindon.

No Country for Old Men is a Thriller. Not an action film. Also, the way you explain it you are saying it’s Llewelyn Moss’ story when in fact it’s the sheriff’s story. Moss thinks that his time as an infantry man in Vietnam is going to enough to thwart his enemies. The sheriff knows he’s in over his head and tries to protect Moss. When he can’t save moss he blames himself. He feels old and like he can’t keep up with modern deviance in society. This is what causes him to retire.
